name: Jovian chromophore, an effective index retrieved from Jupiter's spectrum
paper: A. S. Braude, P. G. J. Irwin, G. S. Orton and L. N. Fletcher, "Colour and tropospheric cloud structure of Jupiter from MUSE/VLT: Retrieving a universal chromophore", Icarus 338 (2020) 113589, DOI 10.1016/j.icarus.2019.113589, its values read from the preprint, arXiv:1912.00918v1
source: the preprint's source, https://arxiv.org/e-print/1912.00918v1, SHA-256 6fe0e947bda8c0f6074bb938dbe205ae7249429621e116de285b5b7f2776e790, fetched 2026-10-14, its file jupiter_muse_paper4.tex, SHA-256 96b3dbd706917bd2fd4a75f79c855dd2c9f4060da07ad324938617733390a66c, the table "Tabulated retrieved imaginary refractive index spectra", its first k column, the adopted universal chromophore (chromophore radius 0.05 µm, cloud radius 1 µm, cloud real index 1.42); read as data

Changed: the adopted solution's k reduced onto this grid and extrapolated below 450 nm, with n held at the paper's 1.4; this file is offered under CC BY 4.0
reduction: n linear and k linear in log k in wavelength between the source's rows, onto 380–780 nm every 5 nm, to six significant figures. The table gives k every 50 nm over 450–950 nm, so below 450 nm k is extrapolated linearly in log k from its 450 and 500 nm rows (0.033 and 0.023), since the chromophore absorbs more towards the blue, and n is held. n is the paper's 1.4, which its retrieval fixes at 700 nm (its §4.1); the paper does not say how n varies elsewhere (a Kramers–Kronig shape, presumably, as in the same group's retrievals), and n is 1.4 throughout
standIn: an effective index retrieved from Jupiter's spectrum for an unidentified colouring material (Braude et al. 2020), not a laboratory measurement
